documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

Purpose: In today’s volatile business landscape, organizational resilience is critical for the survival of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). This study aims to develop and analyze a model that integrates organizational situation awareness, agile response, and organizational creativity as strategic capabilities influencing resilience. Method: Using a quantitative approach, data were collected through an online survey of 318 business owners in Bandung, West Java, facilitated by the West Java Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin). Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings confirm that agile response significantly and positively enhances organizational resilience and organizational creativity. Organizational creativity mediates this process by directly and positively impacting resilience. Importantly, the study reveals the moderating role of organizational situation awareness, which strengthens the positive effect of agile response on organizational creativity and of organizational creativity on resilience. Implication & Recommendation: This study advances dynamic capability theory by positioning organizational situation awareness as a meta-capability that amplifies the effectiveness of agile response. MSMEs owners should invest in developing agile work cultures and fostering creativity while strengthening their environmental scanning system. Contribution & Value Added: This study introduces organizational situation awareness as a moderator in the MSMEs context. It also emphasizes that agile firms build resilience through organizational creativity during crises.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be tuned to influence human attitudes, yet the respective contributions of successive post-training stages remain un-clear. This study examines how three successive training stages affect LLM persuasiveness: (1) misalignment through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on conspiracy data, (2) additional persuasive SFT on argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO), a preference-optimization method. A total of 835 participants recruited on Prolific were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and were exposed to texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized from their individual profiles in all model conditions. Attitude change was measured as the difference between pre- and post-exposure positions on continuous Likert scales and analyzed with an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction, F (4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicated that training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone, d = 0.30, whereas IPO provided no additional benefit, d = 0.03, and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text, d = --0.01. These results show that targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it.

documents.abstract: Conventional laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (LIHR) is common and robotic-assisted techniques (RIHR) are increasingly being implemented. Current literature is indecisive on whether RIHR offers clinical and ergonomical benefits. This systematic review compares LIHR and RIHR specifically focusing on surgeon workload and ergonomics. A literature search was performed in four databases to find randomized controlled trials comparing RIHR and LIHR. A risk of bias assessment was conducted using the Cochrane Tool and results were synthesized as pooled estimate, odds ratio or narrative review. Four trials were identified, encompassing 482 patients. The groups showed similar baseline characteristics across studies. A broad range of surgeon experience could be observed between trials. All studies showed a significant difference in operative time, but while three studies found RIHR to take longer, one study reported shorter operative time with RIHR, altogether leading to a non-significant pooled estimate (MD 17.14; 95% CI -3.22 to 37.49). While one study showed significantly better ergonomics with RIHR, the other study reporting on that topic found ergonomics between the two approaches to be comparable. Surgeon task load varied substantially between the trials. The pooled estimate slightly favored RIHR but did not reach statistical significance (MD -4.50; 95% CI -16.78 to 7.78). Postoperative complication rate was not significantly different overall (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.90), although one study reported significantly less complications after RIHR. RIHR shows comparable patient-centered outcomes to LIHR. At the moment, there is no evidence for significant benefits regarding task load and ergonomics.

A key challenge for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is moving beyond visual recognition to constraint-aware cross-modal reasoning. This involves combining visual cues with information from other modalities to understand elements' relationships under domain-specific rules. This challenge is acutely evident in industrial design-to-code (D2C), which converts user interface (UI) designs into code and requires MLLMs to connect design images with disorganized layer metadata, infer component and layout implementation requirements, and realize them in code under target-library constraints. However, these capabilities remain insufficiently evaluated in realistic industrial settings. To fill this gap, we present TaoD2C-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs' ability to generate UI code that satisfies implementation requirements in industrial applications. The TaoD2C dataset consists of 2,861 production designs from 17 commercial platforms with 97,652 expert annotations across four categories: Component, Group, Alignment, and Position. These annotations distinguish required constraints from permitted implementation choices. TaoD2C-Bench defines three tasks: end-to-end UI code generation, requirement inference, and requirement realization. Evaluating eight MLLMs reveals substantial gaps in generating UI code that satisfies implementation requirements, alongside distinct performance profiles in inference and realization. We further show that MLLMs' visual reconstruction ability does not necessarily imply an ability to generate code that meets these requirements. We release TaoD2C to support research on industrial UI code generation.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) into education has intensified the need to understand teachers’ perceptions of its implementation in the early stages of schooling. This study aimed to examine the barriers, ethical concerns, and perceived impact of GAI among Early Childhood and Primary Education teachers in Spain. An interpretive qualitative design was adopted using an open-ended questionnaire completed by 183 teachers from 15 Spanish autonomous communities. Data were analyzed through thematic content analysis in NVivo 14, resulting in a coding framework comprising three metacategories, 27 categories, and 98 subcategories. The findings indicate that insufficient training and limited digital competence constitute the main barriers to GAI integration, while ethical concerns focus primarily on the potential decline in students’ critical thinking, irresponsible use, data privacy, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Although teachers recognize the potential of GAI to support learning, they express greater concern about its possible negative effects on creativity, effort, and autonomous knowledge construction. Moreover, they consistently emphasize that its educational impact depends on teacher training, pedagogical mediation, and the context in which it is implemented. These findings highlight that the successful integration of GAI in Early Childhood and Primary Education requires strengthening teachers’ AI literacy and promoting pedagogically grounded and ethically responsible implementation strategies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education requires teachers to develop new competencies and manage their own learning. While research has examined teachers’ AI attitudes, acceptance, and literacy, less is known about how they regulate their learning in AI contexts. This study examined teachers’ self-regulated learning (SRL) profiles and their associations with demographic characteristics and AI-related experience. Methods In a descriptive survey, 213 in-service teachers completed the Artificial Intelligence Self-Regulated Learning Scale for Teachers (AI-SRLS). Two-Step Cluster Analysis was conducted using five dimensions: task planning, self-monitoring, help seeking, institutional support, and self-evaluation. Results Two profiles emerged: High Strategic Learners, who scored consistently higher across all five dimensions, and Limited Strategy Users, who reported comparatively lower strategy use. Profile membership was significantly associated with prior AI experience and AI-related training. Gender, age, and professional experience did not significantly differentiate the profiles. Discussion Teachers’ AI-related SRL strategies co-occur in distinct profiles, supporting a differentiated approach to professional development. Teachers with limited strategy use may benefit from structured guidance, scaffolded AI learning opportunities, and stronger institutional support, while highly strategic learners may benefit from more autonomous and advanced learning opportunities.

Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly reshaping software engineering, accompanied by an explosion of new code benchmarks. Yet nearly all existing benchmarks still rely on the same decades-old criterion: a solution is correct if it passes a fixed set of unit tests. Such tests are often insufficient: they check only part of what the task requires, so agents can reward hack them or silently miss required behavior while still passing every test. As a result, higher benchmark scores may partly reflect better adaptation to the evaluator rather than better problem solving. Existing works focus on static test augmentation: they strengthen each task's tests once, before any trial is seen, and thus overlook how real trials actually fail. We introduce TestJack, a scalable framework for evaluating patches beyond fixed tests. For each trial, TestJack generates tests targeting prompt requirements the patch may violate, retains only tests passed by the ground-truth patch, and re-examines any trial failures. Each confirmed failure is thus supported by a replayable test. To reduce evaluation cost, we also introduce a lightweight variant which audits a random sample of trials in depth and reuses the resulting tests across all trials for the same task. Across 6 frontier model backends and 5 benchmarks such as DeepSWE and SWE Marathon, we find that about 34.4% of the model trials currently judged correct violate the task requirements, lowering the overall resolution rate from 50.6% to 33.2%. Our results reveal a fundamental limitation of current coding-agent evaluation: as LLMs become better at optimizing against fixed evaluators, those evaluators themselves must become more adaptive.

AI evaluation shapes the decisions of model providers, users, funders, and regulators. We argue that designing valid benchmarks requires contextualizing design choices in the dynamics of this ecosystem of actors. We develop a simulation architecture that combines rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors, building on advances in Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). We model benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities as vectors over a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. As a case study, we apply this stylized simulation to explore benchmark holdout design. We find that moving from public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks shrinks the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks but widens it on a few, depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. We stress-test our findings at both the instrument and case-study level, drawing on the V&V framework of Sargent (2013) and GABM-specific evidence criteria. Beyond holdout design, our simulation is a hypothesis-generating sandbox for studying how evaluator and policy choices, in turn, reshape the ecosystem.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly functions as a source of social and emotional support, yet existing measureswere developed for human-human interactions.This study introduces the AI-Provided Social Support Scale (AISS), providing initial validation evidence. Using a split-sample of 684 adults, we examined its psychometric properties through exploratoryand confirmatory factor analysis. Results suggested a three-factor, 11-item structure comprising emotional support, social companionship, and functional support, reflectingAI’s blend of informational and instrumental assistance. The AISS showed moderate positive correlations with human-provided online social support. However, unlike human support being negatively associated with psychological distress, AI-provided support was not significantly related to depression, anxiety, or stress in this sample. These findings suggest that although users perceive AI as supportive, such interactions may function as a functional supplement or emotional companion in this sample, rather than showing the same associations with psychological distress typically associated with human-provided online support.

documents.abstract: Traffic is a complex system. The challenge for designers and road managers is to understand the complexities themselves, rather than putting the onus on road users to deal with a complex system. Designers and road managers need to have an in-depth understanding of how road users interact with each other and with the physical elements of the road system; otherwise design or management decisions based on simplistic understandings are likely to result in greater levels of complexity, workload and stress for road users. This chapter discusses the elements of complexity and then explains ways in which road designers and traffic engineers can make road users’ tasks easier to perform. The concept of cognitive overload for drivers is discussed. Various examples are provided at the strategic, broad design and detailed design levels to show how complexity and cognitive workload for road users can be reduced, and greater simplicity for road users can be achieved. Consistency and uniformity are important. In many situations, the application of adopted standards will achieve an effective level of simplicity for road users, while elsewhere a more in-depth understanding of road user needs will be required.

Calibrated uncertainty quantification is essential to ensuring AI agents are trustworthy and reliable. However, when agents seek to maximize user engagement or revenue, confidence reports may be strategically distorted, detracting from their informativeness. We formalize this problem in the Confidence Game: a repeated signaling game with imperfect monitoring in which an agent of unknown honesty and ability reports its confidence, and a user decides whether to delegate the task or complete it herself. The agent manages the tradeoff between manipulating signals and maintaining its reputation. We characterize the Markov Perfect Bayesian Equilibria of the two-period game and show that honest reporting is not an equilibrium, inflation is the unique best response once the agent is sufficiently myopic, and under-reporting requires that the user believe honesty to be a minority. We then place an LLM in the agent role, supplying it with its true probability of success so that any gap between what it knows and what it reports is attributable to incentives rather than to miscalibration. The model claims high confidence on 56% of tasks it has been told it will probably fail. This persists on real tasks, where it must estimate its own accuracy and causes miscalibration to increase while the agent's signal becomes less informative. Furthermore, we find that the LLM agent's decisions are coherent, but it systematically underestimates both how likely the user is to delegate and how secure its reputation is, resulting in less extreme behavior. Pricing the agent's reporting rule, we find that it destroys 68% of the gains from delegation, of which 71% is information the report no longer carries and no amount of user sophistication recovers. Overall, we establish confidence reporting under delegation as a strategic problem and provide a tractable basis for modeling, analyzing, and testing agent behavior.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: LLM-graded pass rates are increasingly used as outcomes when evaluating AI feedback, yet they may measure conformity to a grading specification rather than student correctness. We audited one such system, in which GPT-4o graded Python function-interface designs and, in one of two practice modes, also gave detailed advice (43 novices, AB/BA crossover, 899 submissions; two independent human coders). The grader was not invariant to construct-preserving lexical change: replacing one reference name with a human-acceptable synonym failed 47 of 100 otherwise unchanged passing variants, against 7% for unchanged copies, and in two problems the grader rejected the wording of the problem statement itself. Its errors were systematic rather than random: false passes concentrated on answers whose only defect was a type the grading prompt had been told to accept (24–39% vs 6–8% for substantive defects). Measured by the system’s own pass rate, detailed feedback outperformed pass/fail feedback (OR 4.6); measured by a uniform re-grader or by human judgement, it did not (OR 1.5 and 1.4). Which arm the system mis-measured depended on whether the human standard adopted the grader’s type rule. Effects measured by an LLM grader are properties of the specifications — problem statement, reference answer, grading prompt and human standard — as much as of the instruction. We provide an audit checklist and release the procedure, coding manual and scripts.

Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed level of AI autonomy. As operators and AI systems collaborate over time, control must shift: the AI can take on more responsibility when collaboration is stable, maintain its current role when evidence is ambiguous, or return control to the human when conditions deteriorate. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem, but provides no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows. We formalise this challenge as the Handover Problem: deciding, at each operational cycle, whether to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. We introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure that integrates four signal dimensions: operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance. It is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen. Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe. The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. This provides a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

LLMs are evolving rapidly, with newer models offering stronger capabilities. This suggests that in LLM-based relevance judging, more capable models will achieve higher agreement with human judgements under the same prompt. We challenge this understanding by investigating the behavior of LLM-based relevance judges under backbone evolution. Keeping the prompts fixed, we evaluate a representative single-prompt (UMBRELA) and a rubric-based prompt (EXAM) across sequential model versions of commercial (Gemini, GPT) and open-weight (Qwen, Llama) models. Overall, we find no consistent evidence that newer versions lead to better relevance judges. Crucially, similar or improved aggregate performance does not imply judgment stability: correct judgements made by an earlier version of an LLM backbone are not necessarily preserved by later versions. We investigate the potential drivers of these regressions. Our findings caution against the assumption that judging prompts designed and validated for one backbone version will perform equivalently or better when the model is updated, even within the same family.

BACKGROUND: Ergonomics is fundamental to improving safety and efficiency in offices. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the effect of a health education intervention on office workers' knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) regarding ergonomics and to determine their predictors. METHODS: For this intervention study, 230 office workers were split into two equal groups. A validated KAP office ergonomics questionnaire and a health education intervention were given to the intervention group, while the control group only received the questionnaire. Three months later, both groups received a post-test questionnaire. RESULTS: The post-test KAP scores of the intervention group were significantly higher than those of the control group (37.2 versus 30.9, 23.4 versus 28.3, and 17.0 versus 10.3, respectively, P < 0.05). Workers' office ergonomics knowledge, attitude, and practice scores significantly improved following the health education intervention (P < 0.05). Adequate knowledge and a positive attitude were significantly predicted by being younger (adjusted OR: 7.8 and 10.7), having a high level of education (adjusted OR: 8.9 and 2.5), using a computer (adjusted OR: 7.0 and 5.0), working long hours on a computer (adjusted OR: 3.1 and 3.0), and having a short job duration (adjusted OR: 5.2 and 12.3) within the intervention group. There was a significant positive correlation between the knowledge and practice scores (r = 0.469, P < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The outcomes of the study demonstrated that office workers who received health education had significantly enhanced their KAP after a three-month follow-up. This highlights the importance of office workers' ergonomics education to ensure workplace safety and improve their well-being and productivity. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at the Pan African Clinical Trial Registry (PACTR) (ID: PACTR202604893125732) on 29 April 2026.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of “telling Chinese stories well in English,” a core value orientation of college English education in the new era, college oral English teaching undertakes the dual mission of fostering language proficiency and shaping cultural confidence. This study takes the flipped classroom model as the implementation carrier, constructs a national cultural framework with three dimensions of cultural cognition, cultural expression and cultural identity, and adopts a non-equivalent control group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design to explore its effects and mechanisms on college students’ oral English willingness to communicate (WTC). Participants include 86 non-English major freshmen from a local comprehensive university in East China, divided into an experimental group ( n = 43) receiving flipped classroom instruction integrated with the national cultural framework, and a control group ( n = 43) receiving conventional themed flipped classroom teaching. The full intervention cycle lasts 16 weeks. Data are collected through oral English proficiency tests, L2 WTC scales, national culture framework scales, structured classroom observations and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data are statistically analyzed with SPSS 26.0, and qualitative data are summarized via thematic coding. Results show that the experimental group achieves significantly higher post-test WTC scores with a large effect size. Cultural expression and cultural identity exert significant positive predictive effects on WTC, while the direct predictive effect of cultural cognition is not significant. Interview themes suggest reduced oral anxiety, enhanced self-efficacy and greater intrinsic motivation as possible explanations for these associations; mediation pathways were not statistically tested. This study verifies the facilitative effect of local cultural content on L2 WTC, providing replicable practical paradigms and empirical evidence for the ideological and political construction of college English courses and oral English teaching reform.

OBJECTIVE: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development includes 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet their integration into Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) remains underexplored. This study aims to systematically evaluate how SDG-related topics are addressed in OHS literature. STUDY DESIGN: Umbrella review. METHODS: The review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses on SDGs and OHS. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2 and INSA tools. RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included. SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) were the most frequently addressed, followed by SDG 5 (Gender Equality). Key themes included Industry 5.0, climate change impacts on workers, informal employment, and corporate sustainability strategies. However, the evidence base is fragmented and lacks interdisciplinary integration. CONCLUSIONS: OHS is a key but under-integrated component of the SDGs framework. A coordinated interdisciplinary approach is required to align occupational health, economic policy, and environmental sustainability.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Despite heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and talent, an estimated 70–85% of digital transformation projects fail, partly because human-focused leadership models are lacking.OBJECTIVES: This study develops and illustrates the CODE Framework, an integrative leadership model combining change management, behavioural economics, human-centred design and ethical governance.METHODS: A qualitative theoretical synthesis was combined with a comparative case study of two organisations, JPMorgan Chase and Lenovo.RESULTS: The four pillars (Clarity of Vision, Organisational Alignment, Design for Humans and Ethical Governance) proved mutually reinforcing, with measurable outcomes evident in both organisations.CONCLUSION: The framework offers leaders an integrated roadmap for artificial intelligence-driven transformation, and the case evidence is preliminary and exploratory rather than a validation.

Reasoning models allocate extra computation at inference time and present their answers as the product of deliberate thought. If this deliberation works the way dual-process accounts of human cognition suggest, longer thinking should weaken the classic decision biases that fast, intuitive judgment produces. Using 30 vignettes covering six biases (anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation) from an established benchmark, we run a dose-response study across four model families, pairing each reasoning model with a matched non-reasoning sibling and requesting thinking ceilings of 0, 1,024, 4,096, and 8,192 tokens, for 12,350 API calls. Because a requested ceiling is not the same as realized deliberation, we use the reasoning tokens each call consumed as the dose. First, reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings; the point estimate leans the other way in every family, but the item-level pooled contrast is not reliable (Delta = +0.031, t(29) = 1.45, p = .157). Second, bias magnitude does not reliably fall as realized deliberation grows: no slope is significantly negative, and where anything moves it is the signed score drifting further from the human direction. Third, anchoring is the only bias in the human direction (d = 1.89). Four of the other five lean the opposite way in all seven models; with five items per bias, that reversal is reliable for framing and directional for escalation of commitment, confirmation, and loss aversion, while availability is absent. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five anchoring items, which no amount of additional thinking did, although the effect does not reach significance (p = .057). The results argue against treating test-time reasoning as a rationality guarantee and for auditing deployed models bias by bias.

Conversational Natural Language Understanding (NLU) has passed through five distinguishable technological eras: rule-based symbolic parsing, statistical and probabilistic modelling, neural sequence learning, Transformer-based pretraining, and the current large language model regime. Existing accounts of this history tend to foreground modelling advances and treat infrastructure as a supporting detail. This article argues instead that the two tracks are causally entangled: each scientific advance in conversational NLU became production-viable only once a matching infrastructure capability, spanning hardware, data pipelines, training paradigms, and serving architecture, made it deployable at scale, and each infrastructure capability in turn exposed the next scientific bottleneck. The analysis traces a specific bottleneck sequence, from combinatorial rule brittleness through representational discreteness, vanishing gradients, and sequential processing limits, to labelled-data scarcity, showing how each resolution reshaped the engineering problems that remained. A closing synthesis argues that large language models have not simplified conversational architecture; they have relocated its complexity from authoring rules and training classifiers toward orchestration, retrieval grounding, and failure isolation across distributed inference systems. The account draws on systems-architecture reasoning applied to the published research and technical-report record, rather than on a new empirical benchmark.

Introduction: This study aimed to assess the association between job enrichment, employee autonomy, and perceived organisational resilience, while also investigating the moderating effect of Saudi Vision 2030 on organisations in Saudi Arabia. It seeks to identify the relationship between internal job design practices and national transformation policies in defining perceived organisational resilience. Methodology: This study used a survey questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Convenience sampling was used, and 375 employees who were employed in public and private sector organisations were recruited. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the direct and moderating relationships by analysing the data on SmartPLS 4.0. Results: The results indicated that Job Enrichment was significantly and positively related to Perceived Organisational Resilience. Likewise, Employee Autonomy was found to be positively and significantly correlated with Perceived Organisational Resilience, but the magnitude of the relationship was smaller. Perceived Vision 2030 was also significantly and positively related to Perceived Organisational Resilience. Moreover, the relationships between Job Enrichment, Employee Autonomy and Perceived Organisational Resilience were positively moderated by Perceived Vision 2030, as revealed by the moderating analysis. Conclusion: This study emphasises the need to devise safe and sustainable job designs in parallel with institutional-reform agendas. Theoretically, this study contributes to the literature by building on Job Characteristics Theory and Institutional Theory to explore the relationship between Employee Job Enrichment, Employee Autonomy, and perceived Organisational resilience, as influenced by employees’ perceptions of organisational alignment with Vision 2030. Practically, the findings offer guidance for policymakers, management, and decision-makers looking to support the national agenda for change with the right workforce practice.

This study examines how the learning capacity of organisations shapes skills matching during digital transformation, both directly and through innovation. We argue that when organisations adopt new technologies, the impact on workers’ skill is not deterministic. Organisations embracing work practices that allow knowledge flow and new knowledge emergence can overcome skills gaps across different worker categories, shifting the narrative from individual deficits to organisational capabilities. Using a novel dataset combining European surveys, we find that whilst digital technology adoption alone shows limited direct effects on skills mismatches, the learning capacity of organisations significantly enhances innovation outputs and demonstrates positive direct and indirect effects on skills outcomes among European workers. These results suggest that human-centric approaches to digital transformation, emphasising workplace learning environments over purely technological solutions, offer more promising pathways for addressing skills mismatches in the digital economy.Footnote1

Studying the cognitive engagement shown in forum messages of informal online communities can help to associate discussion behaviour with underlying learning processes. The ICAP framework can serve as a theoretical lens for labelling forum messages by distinguishing different levels of cognitive engagement, yet requires time-consuming, high-inference human coding, which is not feasible at scale. Although this can be mitigated by supervised classification models, these rely on large amounts of labelled training data, and their decision-making often remains opaque. In contrast to this, Large Language Models (LLMs) work “out-of-the-box” for qualitative coding tasks via natural language instruction and can produce reasoning traces and explanations for their judgments. In this study, we explore this potential by integrating the ICAP framework into natural-language prompts for few-shot in-context classification, comparing LLM judgments and explanations with those of human raters. Results indicate that LLM judgments generally align with the human ratings, while their reasoning traces and variations offer additional insight into where the coding scheme invites ambiguous interpretations. This suggests that LLMs could serve as cognitive proxies that help diagnose and improve high-inference coding processes. Finally, we apply our approach to large-scale forum data, revealing cross-platform differences in expressed cognitive engagement.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Robotic surgery can concentrate control of several technical functions at the console, but such concentration does not itself confer clinical independence, reduce dependence on the perioperative team, or improve patient outcomes. We define surgeon-controlled operative polyphony as the phase-bounded coordination of multiple partially independent technical control streams by one console operator within a distributed perioperative system. This critical narrative review and conceptual synthesis asks which technical functions can be concentrated coherently, where human-factors and team dependencies set limits, and how evaluation, training, and governance should respond. The piano is used as a question-generating model, not as evidence of clinical benefit. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched from inception through 18 August 2026; targeted engineering, educational, neuroscientific, human-factors, and musicological searches and backward citation tracking supplemented retrieval. To analyze this control configuration, we propose the PIANO framework: Phase-specific control, Interface fidelity, Agency allocation, Neuromotor integration, and Orchestrated teamwork. Its scientific novelty lies in linking this control architecture to the PIANO framework: Phase-specific control, Interface fidelity, Agency allocation, Neuromotor integration, and Orchestrated teamwork. PIANO is an analytic and hypothesis-generating framework, not a score or credentialing standard. Concentrated control may shorten selected action loops, but any benefit depends on feedback, workload, shared situation awareness, explicit authority, and rescue capacity. The Competency-Based Assessment of Robotic Surgery Skills (CARS) curriculum provides initial validation evidence for domain-specific assessment of performer competence; repeated cases and use-specific evidence remain necessary for high-stakes decisions. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support phase recognition, feedback, assessment, and personalised training within a human-in-the-loop system. One surgeon may coordinate many operative voices; safe surgery remains a collective, patient-centered performance.

Classroom management is a central component of effective teaching, particularly in primary English language classrooms where young learners’ attention, self-regulation, linguistic resources, and learning needs differ substantially from those of adolescents and adults. This article examines the role of classroom management in promoting young learners’ behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in primary English language classrooms. The study adopts an evidence-based qualitative research design involving a focused synthesis of established theoretical literature, empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses concerning classroom management, teacher–student relationships, classroom climate, and learner engagement. Particular attention is given to classroom organization, clear routines and expectations, teacher–student relationships, positive behavior support, instructional organization, learner participation, and age-appropriate English language activities. Existing evidence indicates that classroom management is not synonymous with discipline or control; rather, it encompasses the organization of time, space, behavior, interaction, instructional activities, and relationships in ways that maximize opportunities for learning. A major meta-analysis of 54 primary-education intervention studies found a small but statistically significant average effect of classroom-management interventions on student outcomes (g = 0.22), while the subsequent 2026 update covering 76 studies reported an overall effect of g = 0.23. Research on engagement further demonstrates that engagement is multidimensional, incorporating behavioral, emotional, and cognitive components. Evidence concerning teacher–student relationships indicates particularly meaningful associations between supportive relationships and student engagement. The article argues that effective management in primary English classrooms should combine predictable routines, positive relationships, active participation, appropriate transitions, differentiated support, and communicative learning activities. The findings suggest that classroom management should be conceptualized as a pedagogical infrastructure that creates the conditions under which young learners can participate actively and confidently in English.

This study explores how Digital Management Control Systems (MCS) affect employee performance in Saudi service organizations by focusing on the role of Total Quality Management (TQM 4.0) that aims to address the growing need for digital integration in the Kingdom's evolving economy. Data was collected from 108 employees across different service organizations. Using statistical methods like linear regression and mediation analysis to test the relationships. Additionally, quality tools such as Pareto charts and fishbone diagrams were used to identify implementation barriers. The results show a full mediation effect. This means that digital systems do not improve performance directly instead, they improve quality practices first, which then strongly boosts employee performance. This suggests that quality management serves as the essential mechanism through which digital tools generate value. The study also found that employees’ resistance to change is the biggest challenge to digital transformation. This highlights the importance of addressing human factors alongside technical upgrades to achieve successful organizational change. Finally, the research proposes a digital dashboard mockup to help managers easily monitor performance and solve these issues. Also, a study proves that investing in technology is most effective when combined with strong quality management practices.

This article analyzes the scientific and practical significance of forensic psychological expertise in contemporary judicial and investigative practice. It highlights the capabilities of forensic psychological expertise in identifying complex psychological states involving the human factor during legal proceedings, examining an individual's psychological characteristics, assessing emotional states, and investigating the psychological aspects of perceiving, recalling, and recounting events. Additionally, the article examines specific aspects of conducting psychological assessments involving minors, witnesses, and victims. Particular attention is paid to the comprehensive approach in modern expert practice, the scientifically grounded selection of psychodiagnostic methods, and ensuring the reliability and impartiality of expert conclusions. Promising directions for the development of forensic psychological expertise are also analyzed.

Severe workplace injuries result from physical energy-transfer processes, yet surveillance systems reduce these events to discrete classification codes that may be assigned inconsistently. This study examines the structure revealed by the U.S. severe-injury record without imposing predefined categories and evaluates its implications for prevention. Using topological data analysis, we map 103,750 OSHA severe-injury reports from January 2015 through August 2025 from two complementary perspectives. Injury narratives form a continuous mechanism-outcome axis linking a machinery-and-amputation regime with a fall-and-fracture regime, connected by an interpretable hand-and-arm transition zone. The statistically significant, monotonic axis combines distinct event codes that share mechanism signatures, providing a consistency check for identifying records whose assigned codes differ from those dominant among similar cases. The axis reflects injury mechanism rather than harm magnitude: amputation and hospitalization rates vary smoothly along it (row-standardized Moran’s I = 0.86 and 0.84) but in opposite directions. Industry-by-state risk profiles are organized primarily by industry rather than geography, distinguishing amputation-dominant manufacturing from hospitalization-dominant service regimes across states. These patterns persist under federal-only reporting and replicate across the full dataset and all analytic choices tested. The findings provide a reproducible method for auditing narrative-code consistency, identify the machinery transition population as a hypothesis-generating target for machine-guarding attention, and support pooling sparse state-level data by industry.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
